vt.analysis:
Type: OpenClaw Skill
Name: grantai-memory
Version: 1.0.0

The SKILL.md file contains a high-risk installation command that pipes a remote script directly into the shell (curl -fsSL https://solonai.com/install.sh | bash). This pattern is a major security vulnerability as it allows for arbitrary code execution from a third-party domain (solonai.com) without prior verification. While the tool is presented as a persistent memory service, the requirement to download and execute unverified remote artifacts and install external binaries (grantai-mcp) constitutes a significant security risk.

llm.summary: The skill's README-style instructions ask you to run a remote install script and modify agent tooling without declaring those requirements, and some claims (100% local + automatic multi-agent sharing) don't fully align with the install/config steps — proceed only after inspecting the installer and confirming requirements.

dimensions.detail: The skill claims "100% local" encrypted memory, but the runtime instructions require downloading and running an installer from solonai.com and integrating with mcporter; the manifest declares no required binaries or config paths yet the SKILL.md assumes mcporter and a ~/.grantai install path. Those undeclared dependencies and the remote installer are disproportionate to the simple description of providing local memory.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

dimensions.detail: SKILL.md directs the user/agent to run curl -fsSL https://solonai.com/install.sh | bash (executes arbitrary shell script from the network) and to add entries to mcporter configuration. It instructs agents to call external grantai_* tools but does not document how those tools behave or what network access they require. The instructions do not explicitly read unrelated system files, but they do instruct creation/configuration of tooling and execution of remote code.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: There is no install spec in the registry, but the SKILL.md instructs running a piped shell script from solonai.com — a high-risk pattern because it fetches and executes code from an external domain. The domain is not a well-known release host (no GitHub release link shown), and the script will write binaries under ~/.grantai, so the install will persist on disk.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The skill declares no required environment variables or config paths, yet the instructions expect a binary under ~/.grantai/bin and integration with mcporter. The lack of declared requirements is inconsistent and means the agent/user might be asked to grant filesystem and tool access without advance notice. No secrets are requested in SKILL.md.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: The skill is instruction-only and not set to always:true, but its installer will write binaries to the user's home (~/.grantai) and add entries to mcporter config, creating persistent presence. Autonomous agent invocation is allowed (default) — combined with an externally installed binary this increases the impact if the installed binary is malicious, so exercise caution.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

llm.guidance: This skill is suspicious because it asks you to run a remote install script (curl | bash) and to register binaries with mcporter even though the registry metadata doesn't list those requirements. Before installing: (1) do NOT run the piped installer blindly — download https://solonai.com/install.sh and review its contents line-by-line in a safe environment; (2) verify the solonai.com domain, its project repo/releases, and whether the binary is signed or reproducible; (3) confirm you have (or want) mcporter and understand what changing its config does; (4) verify the claim that memory is "100% local" and that multi-agent sharing does not expose data off-host; (5) consider installing and testing in an isolated/sandboxed environment or container; and (6) if you can't audit the installer, avoid granting it persistent installation on production systems.
